title: Designing a social feed like Twitter

facts.text: The system lets users post tweets (text, image or video), follow other users, read a newsfeed of tweets from the people they follow and search tweets, with high availability, minimal latency and scalability.

Extended requirements are metrics and analytics, retweets and favorites; the primer scopes out the Twitter Firehose, visibility-setting filtering, hiding @replies to people the user does not follow, and the hide-retweets setting.
Singh assumes a read-heavy system with 1 billion total users, 200 million daily active users and 5 tweets per user per day, which gives 1 billion tweets per day and about 12K requests per second.
Singh assumes 100 bytes per message, about 100 GB a day, and media in 10 percent of tweets at 50 KB each, 5 TB a day: about 19 PB over 10 years and about 60 MB per second of bandwidth.

The primer instead assumes 100 million active users, 500 million tweets per day, an average fanout of 10 deliveries per tweet, 60 thousand tweets delivered on fanout per second and 100 thousand read requests per second.

Tables hold users, tweets (type, content, userID), favorites, followers (an N:M relation), feeds and feeds_tweets; each service owns its tables, on PostgreSQL or a distributed NoSQL store such as Cassandra.
Post a tweet takes a user ID, content and an optional media URL; follow or unfollow takes a follower ID and a followee ID; get newsfeed takes a user ID and returns the tweets to show.

A microservices architecture scales horizontally, each service owning its data: user, newsfeed, tweet, search, media, notification and analytics services, talking over REST or the lighter gRPC, with service discovery.

Building a feed retrieves the accounts a user follows, fetches their tweets, ranks them by relevance, time and engagement and returns pages; being intensive, feeds are pre-generated in the cache and refreshed periodically.

Pull builds the feed when a follower reloads (fewer writes, more reads); push writes each tweet into followers' feeds at once (more writes); the hybrid pushes for users with fewer followers and pulls for celebrities.

Posting stores the tweet in the author's SQL timeline; the fan-out service finds the followers and inserts the tweet into each home timeline in a memory cache (1,000 followers mean 1,000 inserts) and queues notifications.

Reading the home timeline, the timeline service gets tweet ids and user ids from the memory cache in O(1), then multigets tweet details and user details from the tweet info and user info services in O(n).

Search uses Elasticsearch, built on Lucene: the search service tokenizes the query, normalizes capitalization and converts it to boolean operations, then scatter-gathers the cluster and merges, ranks and sorts the results.

The fan-out service is a bottleneck: users with millions of followers can take several minutes, racing with @replies, so re-order at serve time and skip fanning out highly followed users, merging their tweets in at read time.

Keep only several hundred tweets per home timeline and only active users in the cache, rebuilding from SQL after 30 inactive days; read replicas cannot absorb cache misses, so add federation, denormalization, SQL tuning and NoSQL.
Cache the top 20% of tweets with LRU eviction and paginate; keep media in object storage behind a CDN; for resilience run multiple service instances, load balancers and read replicas.

notes: Singh's traffic section uses 200 million DAU but its high-level estimate table says 100 million (b95d774fb8ad); the worked example follows the traffic derivation. Singh (1 billion tweets/day) and the primer (500 million tweets/day) assume different scales, so each number is attributed. Left out for the 16-fact cap: data partitioning with consistent hashing, retweets, mutual friends, metrics with Kafka and Spark.

title: Feed fan-out models

definition.text: Ways to build each user's feed: push a tweet into followers' feeds when it is posted, pull it when the feed is read, or combine both.

facts.text: Generating a feed is intensive, especially for users who follow many accounts, and publishing a post to every follower's feed is heavy when a user has millions of followers.
Push (fan-out on write): a new tweet is pushed to all followers' feeds immediately, so the system need not scan a user's followers list for updates, but database writes increase.
Pull (fan-out on load): the feed is built and held in memory only when a follower reloads it, which cuts writes, but recent tweets appear only on request and server reads increase.
The hybrid model combines both: users with fewer followers use push, while users with many followers, such as celebrities, use pull.
In the primer's design, pushing a tweet places it in each follower's home timeline in a memory cache, an O(n) operation: 1,000 followers mean 1,000 lookups and inserts.
Fanning out at 60 thousand tweets delivered per second would overload a traditional relational database, so choose a store with fast writes such as a NoSQL database or memory cache.

Fan-out for users with millions of followers can take several minutes, so the primer suggests not fanning out highly followed users and merging their tweets from search into the home timeline at serve time.

title: Feed ranking

definition.text: Scoring each item in a feed by how relevant it is to a specific user, so the most relevant appear first.

facts.text: A feed needs a ranking algorithm that scores each tweet by its relevance to the specific user, using parameters such as relevance, time and engagement.
Facebook's EdgeRank scored each feed item as Affinity × Weight × Decay; affinity is the closeness of the user to the creator, higher when the user often likes, comments on or messages them.
Weight is a value per kind of edge, so a comment can count more than a like; decay lowers the rank of older edges.
Modern ranking uses machine learning models that can take thousands of factors into consideration.

title: Twitter's tweet recommendation pipeline

definition.text: A five-stage pipeline that narrows 500 million tweets to a ranked, filtered and mixed set.

facts.text: The process has five stages: candidate sourcing, global filtering, scoring and ranking, filtering, and mixing.
Candidate sourcing starts with 500 million tweets, and global filtering cuts them down to 1500 candidates.
Scoring and ranking uses a neural network with 48M parameters.
A further filtering stage achieves author and content diversity, and the final mixing stage blends the tweets with ads recommendations and Who to Follow.

notes: Based on Twitter's open-sourced algorithm as summarized in a short ByteByteGo guide; the Twitter Blue boost mentioned in the scoring stage (5334af70406a) is a product detail and left out.

title: Twitter's technology stack

definition.text: The languages, frameworks, caches and databases behind Twitter's clients and services.

facts.text: Twitter's mobile apps use Swift and Kotlin, with a PWA, and its web client uses JavaScript, React and Redux.
Services run on Mesos with Finagle.
Caching uses Pelikan Cache and Redis, and the databases are Manhattan, MySQL and PostgreSQL.

title: Elasticsearch

definition.text: A distributed, open search and analytics engine, built on Apache Lucene, for storing, searching and analyzing large volumes of data quickly.

facts.text: Traditional databases are sometimes not fast enough to store, search and analyze huge volumes of data in near real time with results in milliseconds; Elasticsearch addresses this.
Elasticsearch is a distributed, free and open search and analytics engine for textual, numerical, geospatial, structured and unstructured data.
It is built on top of Apache Lucene.

In the primer's design the Lucene search cluster is scatter-gathered: every server is asked for matches, then results are merged, ranked, sorted and returned, with tweets kept in memory to keep latency low.

title: Trending topics

definition.text: Showing the queries, hashtags and topics searched most often in a recent window.

facts.text: Trending functionality is built on top of search.
Cache the most frequently searched queries, hashtags and topics from the last N seconds and refresh them every M seconds with a batch job.
The ranking algorithm can also weight trending topics and personalize them for the user.

notes: Two Singh case studies (Twitter, Netflix) describe it in a few sentences; no page of its own.
